# Strain release through hydrogen bond–mediated layer twisting

**Authors:** Qi Zheng; Boyang Li; Sizhan Liu; Chuntian Cao; Jessica M Rimsza; Qiubo Zhang; Jianming Bai; Chun Chang; Jiawei Wang; Chengyao Liang; Haiyan Mao; Matthew R Carbone; Deyu Lu; Tatiana Pyatina; Haimei Zheng

## Abstract

Strain engineering, enabling the precise control over structure and functional properties, is a key strategy for the design of advanced materials. However, the mechanisms governing strain evolution and release at the nanoscale remain largely unexplored. In this study, we leverage in situ heating transmission electron microscopy and synchrotron x-ray spectroscopy to investigate the strain relaxation pathways of boehmite (γ-AlOOH) at 575 kelvin by revealing real-time structural dynamics. Through tracking the moiré pattern evolution, we identify distinct strain release mechanisms, including layer twisting, defect formation, and domain restructuring. Our neural network potential calculations reveal that energy fluctuations at small twist angles are dominated by an interference-like interaction modulation of hydrogen bonds between boehmite interlayers, with metastable twisted structures corresponding to local minima of the potential energy landscape. This work establishes a previously unidentified paradigm of two-dimensional layer twisting mediated by hydrogen bonding, offering insights into strain-driven transformation mechanisms, and thus may have broad implications for strain in material and earth sciences.

## Abstract

Hydrogen bonds unlock a hidden twist, revealing a powerful and unexpected route for strain release in layered materials.

## INTRODUCTION

Strain in materials is ubiquitous. While conventionally associated with mechanical failure (1, 2), strain is also a powerful tool for tuning material properties at multiple scales from enabling flexible electronics (3, 4) to enhancing semiconductor performance (5, 6) and optimizing catalytic reactivity (7, 8). Strain engineering has unlocked previously unidentified frontiers in materials design, enabling precise control over material properties for advanced applications. For example, strain in the epitaxial growth of halide perovskites can enhance the corresponding device efficiency and stability (9, 10). Elastic strain may also be harnessed to transform diamond from an ultrawide bandgap material into a smaller-bandgap semiconductor (11), expanding its potential for various electronic applications. More intriguingly, applying a strain, e.g., 4% in thin films of IV-VI semiconductors such as PbSe and PbTe, can induce a transition between topological and trivial regimes (12, 13). This phenomenon provides a promising avenue for developing strain-controlled nanoswitches in quantum devices, paving the way for next-generation materials.

Strain is also a crucial part of earth sciences research, where it governs geological processes such as rock deformation (14), mantle dynamics (15), and mineral phase transitions under extreme pressures (16, 17). Studies have revealed how strain influences deep-mantle materials (18), affecting our understanding of planetary evolution.

Despite its critical role in both engineered and natural systems, the underlying mechanisms of strain release in many systems remain largely unexplored. Elastic strain is inherently reversible, yet its release can trigger fascinating structural transformations. For example, strain dissipates through atom rearrangement (19), surface reconstruction (20), and defect formation, such as twinning and dislocations (21, 22), and can even drive phase transitions that reshape material properties.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this work, we establish a multimodal imaging and spectroscopy paradigm that integrates advanced in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and in situ x-ray spectroscopy to investigate strain release pathways in boehmite crystals during thermal heating. Unlike classical two-dimensional (2D) materials such as graphene and molybdenum disulfide, which are held together by van der Waals forces (23), boehmite crystals feature layers connected by hydrogen bonds. This unique bonding mechanism imparts greater structural flexibility (24), offering expanded opportunities for multiple applications (25). As shown in Fig. 1A, synchrotron x-ray diffraction (XRD) is used to resolve the gibbsite/boehmite crystal structure, while low-dose TEM imaging captures morphologies. In addition, 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) (26) combined with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping reveals nanoscale local heterogeneities in both strain distribution and chemical composition.

*Fig. 1.: Multimodal characterization of the gibbsite-to-boehmite transition during heating.(A) In situ synchrotron x-ray and TEM used for TEM imaging, 4D-STEM, and chemical mapping. (B) Spatial element maps of Al/O distribution in a single platelet at different heating temperatures. (C) Crystal structure of boehmite from different perspectives. Atomic structures of boehmite resolved using low-dose, high-resolution TEM from (D) the [001] and (E) the [010] zone axis, with the inset showing the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern.*

The boehmite crystals studied here are formed via in situ heating–induced gibbsite transformation. The gibbsite-to-boehmite [α-Al(OH)3 → γ-AlOOH] transition is a crucial geological phenomenon occurring at Earth’s surface and in the crust (27), driven by solid-phase transformations (28) among aluminum (oxy)hydroxides (fig. S1). Gibbsite, a hexagonal crystal with distinct (110) facets (fig. S2), exhibits a layered structure assembled by hydrogen bonds (fig. S3). In situ XRD shows that gibbsite begins to dehydrate at 475 K, with boehmite continuously growing until a full conversion (fig. S4). This phase transformation is also evident in element maps, as the Al/O ratios of gibbsite and boehmite differ substantially. Through detailed EDS calibration using alumina references (figs. S5 to S7 and table S1), we could track the single grain–level heterogeneous nucleation and growth of boehmite during the transition (Fig. 1B) along with the average Al/O ratio increases with temperature as hydroxyl groups dissociate (fig. S8).

Thermogravimetric analysis and XRD confirm that dehydration initiates at 475 K, opening at grain corners and discrete domains, possibly due to local strain concentrations or sharp edges (fig. S9). The transformed boehmite crystals expand, merge, and ultimately form larger particles, often incorporating multiple grain boundaries (fig. S10). The resulting boehmite retains a layered structure (Fig. 1C), with reorganized hydrogen bonds linking the layers. Compared to gibbsite, the octahedral units in boehmite are more closely packed, forming double layers of Al-O octahedra. Crystallographically, the monoclinic symmetry of gibbsite transforms into an orthorhombic structure (29), with distinct (200) and (002) lattice spacings (Fig. 1E). Various defects—including stacking discontinuities, grain boundaries, and amorphous interstitials—are also observed in boehmite (Fig. 1D and fig. S11), potentially contributing to further strain release and structural relaxation.

We examined the strain distribution in boehmite plate during phase relaxation using 4D-STEM. This technique captures a 2D convergent-beam electron diffraction pattern at each pixel of a 2D STEM raster scan (Fig. 2A), achieving a beam size of 2 nm (fig. S12), which corresponds to approximately six unit cells of the boehmite crystal. Apart from reconstruction of virtual-aperture images (fig. S13) (30), full diffraction patterns can be used to generate local strain maps (31). Bragg vectors ⟨200⟩ and ⟨002⟩ define the principal strain directions of interest: ϵ11 and ϵ22 correspond to the normal strains along the ⟨200⟩ and ⟨002⟩ directions, respectively, while ϵ12 represents the in-plane shear strain. The local lattice rotation, associated with domain twisting during strain relaxation, is captured by the angular parameter θ. As shown in Fig. 2B, the quasi-hexagonal boehmite nanoplate exhibits well-defined facets, with strain variations reaching up to ±5%. The strain response appears asymmetrical, with a more pronounced ϵ11 along the [200] direction. This may be explained by the greater structural flexibility of the Al-O octahedra along the [200] axis (32). Given that boehmite is not expected to form a perfectly aligned single-crystalline structure, strain is primarily concentrated at the edges and grain boundaries, likely induced by the gibbsite-to-boehmite solid-phase transformation. In addition, orientation mismatches and subtle particle rotations are directly revealed by the twist angle, θ maps. For example, certain domains exhibit increased twisting from 0° to −2.5°, others relax toward 0°, while some maintain their original orientation, highlighting the potential role of layer twisting in the strain release process. After heating at 575 K in a TEM heating holder for 10 min, the boehmite nanoplate exhibits strain relief and domain reorientation across the entire plate, resulting in a more uniform strain distribution (Fig. 2C). Some tiny grains, typically tens of nanometers in size, exhibit higher mobility and gradually coalesce with neighboring grains during the relaxation process (33), possibly through oriented attachment (34). Meanwhile, surface strains are significantly reduced, likely because of vulnerable surface reconstructions (35). Overall, the strain release process is synchronized with layer rotation, as evidenced by the consistent layer rotation map in Fig. 2C.

*Fig. 2.: Strain analysis of boehmite crystal.(A) Schematic of 4D-STEM mapping of local strains in a boehmite crystal by rastering a convergent beam, with corresponding diffraction patterns at each scanning point. A full diffraction pattern is acquired at each real-space probe location (x, y), with a step size carefully chosen to prevent beam-induced damage to adjacent unsampled regions. Bragg vectors ⟨200⟩ and ⟨002⟩ define the strain directions of interest, represented as ϵ11 and ϵ22, respectively. (B) Strain map of a boehmite platelet at 575 K and (C) after a 10-min heating duration at 575 K.*

Magic-angle graphene superlattices have demonstrated unconventional superconductivity in 2D materials (36, 37). Specifically, the misorientation of two stacked layers induces rotational moiré patterns (Fig. 3A) (38). The moiré fringe spacing is notably larger than the atomic lattice spacing, effectively magnifying structural variations (Fig. 3B). Conversely, the twist angle can also be determined from the moiré spacing, with larger spacings corresponding to smaller twist angles. Moiré lattices emerge during the gibbsite-to-boehmite transformation, absent in pristine low-strain gibbsite but widespread in boehmite product (fig. S14). Their presence serves as a reliable indicator for strain visualization.

*Fig. 3.: Strain release through layer twisting during in situ heating.(A) Schematic illustration of moiré pattern formation due to the twisting of 2D layers. (B) Moiré patterns in boehmite at different twist angles. (C) TEM image of moiré patterns formed by two mismatched boehmite layers, where the top layer rotates ~5° clockwise relative to the other. The inset shows the selected area diffraction pattern with two distinct sets of diffractions. (D) Intensity profiles of two distinct moiré patterns at different lattice spacings: The 4.0-nm pattern originates from the twisting of the {100} lattice of the boehmite crystal, while the 8.5-nm pattern corresponds to the {001} lattice. (E) Theoretical calculation of moiré pattern spacing as a function of twist angle. (F) Evolution of moiré patterns during strain release, with different domains highlighted in color. (G) Quantitative analysis of moiré pattern pathways, including pattern area (S), lattice spacing (d), orientation (Φ), and layer twist angle (θ). The colors in (D) and (E) represent different domains, and the error bars are calculated from multiple domain measurements.*

Selected area electron diffraction reveals that two boehmite layers are directly stacked, producing two distinct diffraction patterns with a measured twist angle of 4.5° (Fig. 3C). Two types of moiré patterns are observed in boehmite, corresponding to different crystallographic planes. In detail, the 4.0-nm moiré lattice originates from the (100) plane, while the 8.5-nm pattern is assigned to twisting of the (001) plane (Fig. 3D). Since the (100) and (001) planes are perpendicular, their resulting moiré superlattices also form perpendicular patterns, providing evidence of their origins. Moiré spacings can be predicted using known lattice planes and their d-spacings. In Fig. 3E, we calculate the moiré spacing as a function of twist angle for the (100) and (001) planes. Our calculations yield a consistent twist angle of 4.7° ± 0.5°, which aligns well with experimentally measured values, also supporting the formation of moiré lattices from these planes.

Inspired by moiré superlattices, we capture the real-time layer twisting dynamics of boehmite at 575 K. Using in situ TEM, we identify a previously unidentified mode of strain release driven by layer twisting at local domains (movie S1). The moiré pattern reveals layer mismatches associated with strain, and as additional lattice planes intersect, along with the intrinsic grain boundaries in boehmite, the complexity of the moiré pattern increases, substantially influencing local strain distribution (fig. S15). We identify four distinct sets of moiré lattices at different spacings, highlighted in different colors (Fig. 3F and movie S2). Initially, these patterns are concentrated on the boehmite surface and exhibit high mobility, propagating because of local layer twisting (20 s). Eventually, they merge and dissipate, indicating a rapid strain release process through layer twisting. Quantitative analysis in Fig. 3G shows that the moiré pattern (S) evolves rapidly; the propagation rates of specific moiré pattern can reach up to 160 nm2/s, while some patterns evolve more slowly, at approximately 50 nm2/s. Such phenomena are likely influenced by the specific lattice planes involved, also observed in faceted etching propagation (39). Meanwhile, the twisting angles (θ) can be determined from the moiré spacings (d), revealing clear fluctuations in the layer twisting angles within a range of 5° to 10°. We also notice the orientation (Φ) of patterns can adjust dynamically, possibly because of localized granular rotation—an effect also observed in the deformation of metallic materials (40, 41).

We further resolve the distinct modes of moiré pattern evolution during the strain release process (movie S3). One predominated mode is fast propagation, where the moiré lattice migrates directionally while maintaining a constant orientation (Fig. 4A). Another mode involves shuffling and local fluctuations in Fig. 4B, where the moiré patterns undergo minor oscillations and adjustments, enabling strain energy dissipation through localized vibrations. In addition, larger moiré domains can split into smaller regions with increased mobility, allowing for more efficient strain redistribution. However, structural defects such as grain boundaries can disrupt this process. As illustrated in Fig. 4C, moiré lattices can become trapped and stabilized at grain boundaries, preventing further migration. These different modes of pattern evolution appear to be correlated with the local strain magnitude, which dictates whether the moiré structures dissipate, stabilize, or expand in response to the strain field.

*Fig. 4.: Various modes of moiré pattern during the strain release process.(A) Fast propagation, (B) local fluctuation, and (C) splitting and trapping at the grain boundary.*

To understand the thermodynamics of the moiré pattern, we simulated a set of patch models under periodic boundary conditions, consisting of isolated patches overlaid on an infinitely large substrate to replicate the experimentally observed twisted structures. In Fig. 5A, both the patch and substrate are composed of double layers of Al-O octahedra, coupled through interlayer hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) that dictate the twist angle–dependent energetics. At the interface, oxygen atoms in the patch and substrate (OI) form offset rectangular sublattices with a 1.43-Å displacement along the a axis; each OI in the patch forms one donor and one acceptor H-bond with OI atoms in the substrate along the c direction, with a mean O···H bond length of 1.61 Å (fig. S16). A machine learning force field (MLFF) was trained on density functional theory (DFT) results from different patch models, achieving root mean square errors of 3.86 meV per atom in energy and 0.198 eV/Å in force (42, 43), in line with DFT-level accuracy (fig. S17). This MLFF was subsequently applied to a larger patch model (8.6 nm by 11.1 nm), consistent with the experimentally observed domain size in Fig. 3C.

*Fig. 5.: Theoretical modeling of twist-dependent energetics in hydrogen-bonded boehmite layers.(A) Side (left) and top view (right) of a twisted boehmite supercell structure (θ = 6°) in the patch model. Black dash lines represent H-bonds between interfacial oxygen (OI, highlighted in yellow) and H atoms. (B) Calculated total energy per patch area (Etot) and number of hydrogen bonds (nH) versus twist angle (θ). (C) Histogram of O⋅⋅⋅H H-bond distance at θ = 6°. Inset illustrates the twisting of the H-bonds at the interface. (D) Etot from different patch models with θ scaled by patch size (l). This universal trend can be explained by a square lattice model based on the displacement of twisted patch OI atoms with respect to their untwisted structure represented by a square lattice. Blue, orange, and green dots in inset represent patch OI atoms in the first, second, and third shells, respectively. The single atom in the first-order shell is the twisting center. (E) Decomposition of Etot from the lattice model contributions from OI atoms in different shells.*

The total energy per unit area, Etot, as a function of twist angle, θ (Fig. 5B) shows a minimum at 0°, a maximum at 4°, followed by damped oscillations with local minima near 6° and 11°. These subsequent minima correspond to metastable twisted structures observed in the 4D-STEM (Fig. 3G), indicating thermodynamic stabilization near 6° and 11°. Etot exhibits an inverse correlation with the number of interfacial H-bonds, nH, especially for θ < 10°, implying that the twisting energetics are largely governed by the structure and dynamics of the interfacial H-bond network. Etot can deviate by approximately 50 meV/Å2 from the untwisted configuration, while variations among twisted structures can reach up to 15 meV/Å2. These energy differences highlight the crucial role of H-bonds in modulating the energetics of twisted boehmite layers. The O···H distance distribution at the interface (Fig. 5C) exhibits a broad peak at 1.66 Å with a substantial standard deviation of 0.22 Å, indicating the dynamic and flexible nature of interlayer hydrogen bonding during twisting (fig. S18). This behavior represents a distinct form of layer twisting, fundamentally different from the moiré patterns reported in van der Waals materials such as graphene (44), hexagonal boron nitride (45), and transition metal dichalcogenides (46). Unlike the weak, nondirectional interlayer coupling in those systems, twisting in boehmite layers arises from a completely different mechanism, as H-bond interactions are directional.

We examined the effect of patch size, l, by constructing twisted boehmite models with l ranging from 1 to 10 nm (fig. S19) and found that Etot shows a strong dependence on patch size (Fig. 5D): Smaller crystallites exhibit slower fluctuations, indicating a softer potential energy surface and, likely, enhanced structure flexibility in layer twisting. As l increases, effectively, the Etot(θ) curve becomes compressed along the θ axis (fig. S20). A universal energy profile, Etot(θ·l), across different patch sizes can be obtained by scaling θ by l. This universal trend rules out any nontrivial changes in the H-bond network topologies across varying sizes. To further interpret this behavior, we developed a simplified lattice model in which the positions of OI atoms in the patch and substrate are approximated by square lattices (figs. S21 and S22). In this model, the H-bond energy is lowest when an OI atom lies at a lattice vertex and highest at the center of a grid cell. The total energy is computed by summing the H-bond energies over all positions, according to the distance of the displacement. This lattice model reproduces the damped oscillatory energy behavior predicted by MLFF (fig. S23). We further define shells based on the radial distance from the twisting center: The first shell contains a single central OI atom, while higher-order shells correspond to “square rings” of increasing sizes (inset in Fig. 5D). Each shell-resolved energy curve exhibits an oscillatory pattern, with peaks when OI atoms are near vertices and troughs when near grid centers (Fig. 5E). At a given θ, atoms in outer shells undergo larger displacements than those in inner shells, leading to oscillations at higher frequencies. Because the number of OI atoms in the nth shell scales as 8·(n − 1), outer shells have bigger weights in Etot. Summing the contributions from all shells—each with distinct amplitudes and frequencies—yields a “wave-like” Etot profile in Fig. 5D, reflecting the constructive and destructive interaction modulation of H-bond network across the interface.

Leveraging advanced characterization techniques, including synchrotron XRD, 4D-STEM, and in situ heating TEM, we gain unprecedented insights into strain evolution at the nanoscale. Our study focuses on strain release pathways in boehmite crystals (movie S4), capturing real-time strain relaxation dynamics and their impact on material stability and transformation mechanisms. A previously unidentified strain release pathway via 2D layer twisting is revealed through tracking the evolution of moiré patterns. Distinct evolution modes are identified, including fast propagation, local fluctuations, and splitting-trapping at grain boundaries. Our neural network potential calculations reveal that energy fluctuations corresponding to the adjacent twist angle variations are strongly influenced by hydrogen bonding between boehmite interlayers, the dynamic nature of interlayer H-bond as well as the interference-like modulation of H-bond interactions can substantially enhance the flexibility of layer twisting. Our findings indicate that similar twisting-mediated strain relaxation may occur in hydrogen-bonded layered materials, suggesting that the mechanism could be broadly applicable. Understanding these processes paves the way for designing strain-tunable materials with enhanced functionalities, offering exciting possibilities for applications in nanoelectronics, energy technologies, and geoscience.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Sample preparation

Commercially available gibbsite (α-Al(OH)3), boehmite (γ-AlOOH), and corundum (α-Al2O3) were used as received. Thin carbon film TEM grids (5 nm, 200 mesh) were purchased from Electron Microscopy Sciences. The powders were dispersed in methanol and drop-cast onto the grids. In addition, hydrothermally synthesized boehmite was used for comparison, exhibiting more pronounced moiré patterns and higher strain (fig. S16). This sample was prepared by mixing gibbsite with 3 wt % sodium metasilicate (Na2SiO3), adding water at a water-to-solid ratio of 1:2, and curing the mixture at 85°C and 99 ± 1% relative humidity for 24 hours. The cured sample was then autoclaved in a Parr Reactor (model 4622, Hillsboro, OR, USA) at 300°C for 30 days (47).

### In situ TEM and EDS mapping

Morphological characterization and chemical mapping were performed on a Thermo Fisher Scientific ThemIS TEM (approximately 1 × 10−7 mbar vacuum pressure measured from IGPco) operated at 300 keV. In situ heating experiments were conducted with a Gatan 652 heating holder, equipped with a tantalum furnace, at a controlled heating rate of 5°C/min. Videos were recorded using a Ceta2 camera at 5 frames per second, with an electron dose rate of ~500 electron/Å2 s−1. The temperature rise induced by the electron beam at such a low dose rate is negligible. Elemental mapping was performed using a Bruker EDS detector with a 0.7-sr solid angle, enabling high count rates with minimal dead time. The dwell time was set to 20 μs with drift correction enabled. For EDS analysis, background correction was performed using a multipolynomial model, and an absorption correction was applied on the basis of an assumed sample thickness of 500 nm and a density of ~3.03 g cm−3. The Schreiber-Wims function was used as the ionization cross-sectional model.

### 4D-STEM and data processing

4D-STEM datasets were collected using a Gatan Orius charge-coupled device on an FEI TitanX microscope operated at 300 kV in microprobe STEM mode, with a convergence semiangle of α = 0.48 mrad and a camera length of 245 mm. The Gaussian-shaped probe had a full width at half maximum of ~2 nm. A beam stop was not used to avoid masking diffraction spots. Diffraction patterns were recorded with a 5-nm step size over an area of 180 pixels by 300 pixels, with an acquisition time of 50 ms per frame. Data processing and analysis were performed using the py4DSTEM Python package (48).

### Synchrotron XRD

Time-resolved in situ synchrotron XRD patterns were collected at beamline 28-ID-1 (PDF) of the NSLS-II at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). The x-ray beam had a wavelength of 0.1665 Å and a spot size of 0.5 mm by 0.5 mm. Gibbsite powder was encapsulated in a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)/quartz reactor and uniformly heated with a coil heater from room temperature to 575 K. The heating temperature was calibrated using a K-type thermocouple. Rietveld refinements of XRD patterns were performed on TOPAS-Academic V7.12 software. A mask was applied to remove dead pixels and beam stop shadows. The refined parameters included background coefficients, zero shift, peak shape parameters, lattice parameters, atomic positional parameters, phase fractions, and isotropic atomic displacement parameters (Uiso). Uiso values of all elements occupying the same crystallographic position were set equivalent.

### DFT calculation

All DFT calculations were performed using Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) (49, 50). The generalized gradient approximation of Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (51, 52) was used to describe exchange-correlation term. A plane wave cutoff of 500 eV was used to identify the lattice parameter, and 300 eV was used for ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulation. The k-points of 1 by 1 by 1 were used in AIMD simulation. The electronic optimization was performed until the total energy difference between two adjacent iterations was less than 10−5 eV.

### Computational model construction

The patch model consists of an isolated patch layer placed atop a periodic substrate layer. For the small patch model, the substrate is constructed as a p(5 × 5) supercell of the boehmite structure, while the patch layer is a p(3 × 3) supercell. Here, p(m × n) denotes an m × n × 1 supercell derived from the original unit cell. The total number of atoms in this system is 272. During AIMD simulations, the top five and bottom five atomic layers are fixed to maintain a constant twist angle, allowing only the interfacial O and H atoms to relax. For the large patch model, which contains 27,200 atoms, the substrate is modeled as a p(50 × 50) supercell and the patch as a p(30 × 30) supercell. Structure relaxation was performed under various twist angles, with the same constraint applied to the outermost five layers. Details on the commensuration construction are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

### MLFF training

Our MLFFs were trained on-the-fly during AIMD simulations using a canonical ensemble (NVT) with a time step of 1 fs implemented in VASP (53). The cutoff radius for the three-body descriptor and the width of the Gaussian functions used for broadening the atomic distributions of the three-body descriptor were set to 6 and 0.4 Å, respectively. The maximum number of local configurations (ML_MB in VASP) was set as 2000 for each element. The training was performed on small patch model under twist angle from 0 to 15 with step of 1. Each simulation will run at 300 K for 500 steps. Eventually, dataset include 850 DFT calculations, and the model was refitted for fast prediction.
